GMI = 3.31 + 0.02392 × mean glucose (mg/dL). Estimated A1C = (mean glucose + 46.7) / 28.7. Both are estimates calculated from sensor readings, not laboratory measurements, and they legitimately disagree with each other and with a blood test.

This app is not a medical device and it is not a source of truth. It reads glucose values from your LibreLinkUp account and shows them. It does not measure anything itself.

Do not make treatment decisions on what you see here. If a number matters — if you are deciding whether to eat, dose or drive — check the official FreeStyle Libre app or scan your sensor. If this app and the official app disagree, the official app is right and this one is wrong.

Values can be wrong, late, or missing. They pass through Abbott\'s servers, your network and Android\'s background limits before reaching this screen, and any of those can delay or drop them. A number on screen with no warning beside it still only means "this is the most recent value we managed to fetch".

Alarms can fail to arrive. Android may delay or suppress notifications while the phone is asleep, in Do Not Disturb, or saving battery, and this app cannot override all of that. Never rely on it to wake you. Treat a silent night as no evidence that nothing happened.
If you feel unwell, believe what your body is telling you over what this app shows, and seek medical advice. Nothing here replaces your clinician.

Typeface, size, spacing and zone colours.
Drawn so no character can be mistaken for another: 1 and l, 0 and O, 6 and 8. Made for low vision, and the most useful here because this app is mostly three digits read at a glance.

Weighted letter bottoms. The controlled evidence is weak: a 2017 study found it reduced reading speed and accuracy against ordinary fonts. Offered because preference counts too, not as a recommendation.
Size and spacing help more than the choice of typeface does, and they help everyone. Worth trying before changing font.

Uses the phone\'s light or dark setting, including any automatic schedule.
Always dark, even when the phone is light. Useful if you check your glucose at night.
Red low, green in range, amber high: the LibreLink convention.
Okabe–Ito palette: warm low, green in range, cool high. Separates the zones along the blue–yellow axis instead of red–green, and stays readable in greyscale.
The same logic in deeper tones, for low vision or screens read in sunlight.
Colour is never the only cue: zones also differ by position, label and shape.

The dashed line is an estimate of where glucose might go, worked out from recent readings. It can be wrong, and it is wrong more often the further ahead it looks. Do not use it to decide a dose or to treat a low \u2014 for that, the official app and a fingerstick.
This appears every time you open the app with the projection on, deliberately.

This app reads your LibreLinkUp data through an unofficial API and can fail or lag without warning. Alarms may not sound if the phone is asleep, in Do Not Disturb or saving battery. For any medical decision, Abbott\'s official app is the one that counts.

Each hour of the day, gathered across the period. The line is the median; the strong band is the middle 50% of readings and the pale one reaches from the 10th to the 90th percentile. What this shows is not only where each part of the day sits, but how much it varies.

See your readings from a browser
The phone sends each reading to a server you host, so it can be read from a browser. The server keeps no history: only the latest value, in memory, and it forgets that on restart.
The same key goes on the server (CGM_RELAY_SECRET) and is asked for once in the browser.
Without https the key and your readings cross the network in clear.
This is the only feature that sends data off the phone. While it is on, your latest value also exists on that server. Anyone holding the key can read it.

If xDrip+ is already reading your sensor, this app can take its readings from there: any sensor xDrip+ supports, with no account and no password. It has to be switched on in xDrip+ (Settings → Inter-app settings → Broadcast locally, with Compatible Broadcast).
Abbott\'s cloud. Polled about once a minute, and it needs your follower account.

Switch it on inside xDrip+: Settings → Inter-app settings → "Broadcast locally", with "Compatible Broadcast". If it is off, this app receives nothing and cannot tell: readings simply never arrive.

A walk through every screen, and what each one will not tell you
Opens the screen. Press back to come straight back here.

Thirteen short steps through what each screen does — and, as often, what it deliberately does not do.

One thing first, because everything else rests on it: this app describes what happened. It never suggests what to do. It is not a medical device, it has been assessed by no regulator, and the readings come from a consumer sensor through an interface its maker does not support. Treat every number here as a description, not an instruction.

You can leave at any time, and reopen this from Settings.

Two choices, and they are alternatives — only one is live at a time.

**LibreLinkUp** reads the sensor maker's own follower cloud. It needs your account, and it adds the cloud's own delay to each reading.

**xDrip+** takes whatever that app is already reading, over a local broadcast on this phone. No account, no password, no network — and it works with any sensor xDrip+ supports, which is most of them. It has to be switched on inside xDrip+ first; the Settings screen says exactly where.

This is the first stop because every number on every later screen depends on it.
The number, and how old it is

The current reading, large, with an arrow for where it is heading and the change since the last one — shown over the span it covers, because a rise of 14 means something different over five minutes than over twenty.

Underneath it, the thing most apps leave out: **how old the reading is**. The colour fades as it ages and says so plainly when it has gone stale. A number with no age on it is a number you cannot act on, and the whole chain here — sensor, phone, cloud — takes time.

The same figure sits in the status bar, so you rarely have to open the app at all.

Pinch to zoom from an hour out to a week. Drag sideways to go back through history — the clock along the bottom follows, and the tick crossing midnight carries its date, so yesterday never looks like this morning.

Tap any point for its exact value and time. While you are browsing, a **Now** button appears on the chart to bring you back to the present in one tap; reopening the app always returns there by itself.

The trace breaks wherever nothing was recorded. It would be easy to draw a line across the gap, and that line would be invented.

High, low, urgent low, and one for **signal loss** — because a feed that has quietly stopped is the failure that matters most and the one you are least likely to notice.

Each alarm has its own threshold, each can be switched off, and each can be set to sound through Do Not Disturb independently. A low at three in the morning and a high after lunch are not the same kind of event, so they do not have to behave the same way.

Nothing predicted ever triggers an alarm. Only a measured reading does.

The band the app treats as in range, and the edges beyond it.\n\nIt starts from your account\'s own targets so the colours agree with the app you already use. Override them here and the override is re-applied to every reading that arrives, including the ones already drawn — so the chart, the statistics, the exported report and the watch can never disagree about what counts as high.

Insulin and food, as you record them. Doses to the half unit, carbohydrates in grams, with the usual amounts one tap away.

The time recorded is when the dose was **given**, not when you typed it, because entering a forgotten injection from yesterday is an ordinary thing to do and putting it on today's timeline would make the chart lie.

Entries here are editable. A mistyped dose has to be correctable.

Every reading the sensor produced, in order, grouped by day.\n\nThis is the counterpart to the Diary and the distinction is the only thing worth knowing about the two screens: the Logbook is what was **measured**, and nothing in it can be edited. A corrected reading would be a falsified record.

Pick a window from a day to three months. GMI and estimated A1C first, then time in range as one bar you can read at a glance.

Above all of it sits **coverage** — how much of that window was actually recorded. A confident-looking 90-day figure resting on six days of data is the exact way these screens mislead, so the figure that governs how to read everything else comes first.

Below, the shape of a typical day, twice: a ribbon across the 24 hours and the same percentiles as box plots. Slide a finger across either to read a slice, or tap to open it full screen — turn the phone sideways there and a day gets the width it deserves.

At the foot of the Trends tab. Choose a period from a week to a year, cut it by day, week or month, and get mean and median side by side for each range.

Both, not one: glucose has far more room above target than below it, so the two part company whenever a stretch runs high — and that gap is itself the finding.

Ask for several **figures per day** and each range reports every few hours instead of once, which is what shows *when* in the day it comes apart. Export as CSV, JSON or HTML, or print it to a PDF. Every format carries the thresholds, the coverage and the disclaimer, because a file gets read months later by someone who was not there.

A dyslexia-friendly typeface or a high-legibility one, text and spacing you can enlarge, and palettes for the common kinds of colour blindness.

The typeface follows through to the number in the status bar and the car display — the places you actually read it from, rather than only the screen where you chose it.

Colour is never the only carrier of meaning here. Every zone has a position and a figure as well as a hue.

Daily reminders at a fixed time for a dose that is easy to forget, delivered to the phone and to the watch.\n\nThey use exact alarms, and if Android has not granted that permission the app says so rather than letting you discover it from a reminder that arrived forty minutes late.

Each of these is a decision, not something missing.

**Nothing backfills.** The upstream service serves about half a day of coarse history, so every long window fills up from the day you installed this and not before. That is why coverage is on every screen that shows a figure.

**It never suggests a dose**, and no prediction can trigger or silence an alarm.

**Nothing leaves the phone** unless you switch on the web relay, which holds one value in memory on a server you run and forgets it on restart.

The forecast is switched off. It will come back when it can state how often it was right.

That is the tour. It is in Settings whenever you want it again.
Tap the bar for each band\'s boundaries and how long was spent in it.
The percentages are of the readings that exist, not of the calendar. The time beside each one is per recorded day: where coverage is partial, the hours nobody measured count towards nothing.
%1$d ranges with no readings at all were left out. The row above still covers the whole period, gaps included.

Repeats the alarm as a message, the only shape Android Auto surfaces. The car reads it aloud, to passengers as well as you.
